questions.text: After tokenising with unnest_tokens(), anti_join(stop_words) is applied. What does this step remove?
options: Common, high-frequency words that carry little meaning (e.g. 'the', 'and', 'is')
Words that appear in only one document
questions.explanation: Stop words are high-frequency function words (the, and, is, of, etc.) that appear in virtually every document and thus carry no discriminating information. Removing them improves the signal-to-noise ratio in downstream analyses.

questions.text: TF-IDF gives a high score to a word that:
options: Appears in every document in the corpus
Appears frequently in a specific document but rarely across all documents
Appears exactly once in the entire corpus
questions.explanation: TF-IDF = TF × IDF. High TF means the word is frequent in the document. High IDF means it is rare across documents. The product is highest for words that are characteristic of a specific document or group.

questions.text: A word that appears equally in all plan tiers will have a high TF-IDF score when plan_tier is used as the document.
questions.explanation: If a word appears in all documents (plan tiers) with similar frequency, its IDF will be close to 0 (DF ≈ N), making TF-IDF ≈ 0. TF-IDF rewards words that are distinctive, not ubiquitous.

questions.text: The Document-Term Matrix (DTM) produced by cast_dtm() is described as 'sparse'. This means:
options: Most entries are 0 because most documents do not contain most terms
It has fewer rows than columns
It is stored as a dense numeric matrix
questions.explanation: A sparse matrix has mostly zero entries. In a DTM, most documents use only a small fraction of the total vocabulary, so most (document, term) entries are 0. Sparse storage formats save memory by recording only non-zero entries.

questions.text: bind_tf_idf() in tidytext requires three arguments. Which are they?
options: document, term, n (count per document-term pair)
questions.explanation: bind_tf_idf(term, document, n) takes the term column name, the document column name, and the count column (n = occurrences of the term in that document). It adds tf, idf, and tf_idf columns.
